nameStory: The wild daffodil gets its 'wild' name to distinguish it from the countless garden varieties bred from it over centuries. It's also called the Lent lily because it blooms during the Christian season of Lent in early spring, bringing hope after winter's end.
description: Wild daffodil is a cheerful spring bulb that produces the classic yellow trumpet flower we all recognize. It grows 6-12 inches tall with narrow, grayish-green leaves that emerge straight from the ground around the flower stem. Unlike many garden daffodils, wild daffodils have softer, paler yellow petals surrounding a deeper yellow central trumpet, giving them a more delicate appearance than their bold garden cousins.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single pale yellow flower with six outer petals (tepals) surrounding a darker yellow trumpet-shaped center that you could imagine a tiny fairy using as a megaphone

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, strap-like leaves with a distinctive grayish-green color that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, rising directly from ground level

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows from an underground bulb, typically forming small colonies over time, with each plant producing a single flower on its own stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers nod slightly downward and have a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's strongest on warm sunny days

habitat: In New England, wild daffodils are typically found as garden escapes in old homesteads, abandoned farmsteads, and naturalized areas near former settlements. They prefer well-drained soils in partial shade to full sun, often appearing in old orchards, woodland edges, and meadows where they've spread from long-forgotten plantings.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom in early to mid-spring, typically March through April, with gray-green leaves emerging just before or with the flowers. This is prime identification time when the distinctive pale yellow trumpets are unmistakable.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain green through late spring and early summer, slowly yellowing and dying back as the plant stores energy in its underground bulb for next year's show.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground, though new bulbs may be forming underground from this year's seed production.
seasonality.winter: No visible growth above ground, existing only as dormant bulbs beneath the soil waiting for spring's warming temperatures.

funFact: Wild daffodil flowers that grow from seeds take an incredible five to seven years to produce their first bloom, which means that cheerful flower you're admiring may have been patiently growing underground since you were in elementary school!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with garden daffodil varieties, but wild daffodils have distinctly paler, more delicate yellow petals compared to the bold, bright yellow of most cultivated types. Memory trick: 'Wild and mild' - the wild ones have milder, softer colors.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'wild,' these daffodils in New England are actually naturalized plants that escaped from colonial and early American gardens. True wild populations are native to Western Europe, so our New England 'wild' daffodils are really just very old garden escapes that have learned to fend for themselves.
compareHints: Wild daffodil differs from its Narcissus relatives by having pale yellow petals rather than the pure white of Poet's Narcissus or Paperwhite, and produces single flowers rather than the clusters seen in Bunch-flowered Daffodil. The trumpet is also proportionally larger and more prominent than in most other narcissus species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the familiar yellow trumpet daffodils (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) that bloom earlier, poet's narcissus has pure white petals and a flat, small center rather than a large trumpet.
Unlike wild daffodil which has one large flower per stem, this species always has multiple smaller flowers clustered together.

Unlike other daffodils in New England, the hoop-petticoat has an enormous corona that completely dominates tiny, thread-like petals - the exact opposite of poet's narcissus which has huge white petals and a tiny orange cup.
Unlike other New England daffodils that bloom singly in spring with thick, substantial petals, paperwhite produces clusters of smaller flowers with distinctively thin, translucent petals.
Angel's-tears differs from other New England daffodils by its tiny size, pure white color, and distinctly drooping flowers.
